phases.title: A new province
phases.story: Claudius's army landed in AD 43 and within a generation much of lowland Britain was a Roman province. The written record is Roman and hostile to the Britons; the ground adds burnt towns from Boudica's revolt, new ports and palaces, and letters from the army on the northern frontier.

phases.title: Walls, towns and villas
phases.story: From the 120s a wall ran across northern England; for a time in the 140s and 150s the frontier moved north to the Antonine Wall before settling back on Hadrian's line, and the lowland province settled into towns, villas and roads. Walls and roads are lines the atlas cannot yet draw, so this chapter is thin on the map; the evidence for it is plentiful on the ground.

phases.title: Late Roman Britain
phases.story: In the fourth century Britain was a wealthy, largely peaceful part of the empire, and Christianity reached its villas and treasures. As imperial control weakened after 400, people buried their valuables and, by about 410, Roman government had ended.

phases.title: After Rome
phases.story: The two centuries after Rome are the least documented in British history. Almost no contemporary writing survives, so what we know comes mostly from archaeology: imported pottery in the west, new burial customs in the east, and later writers looking back.

phases.title: Kingdoms and conversion
phases.story: By the seventh century Britain was a patchwork of kingdoms whose rulers were buried with extraordinary wealth. Christian missions from Rome and Iona brought monasteries, books and a written history, much of it from Bede, writing in Northumbria.

phases.title: Norse settlement and the making of England
phases.story: From 793 Scandinavian raiders, then armies and settlers, reshaped Britain. Kings of Wessex fought, bargained and expanded until a single English kingdom emerged, which in 1066 was fought over by Norwegian and Norman claimants.
